memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "He said to Aaron, 'Take a bull calf for your sin offering and a ram for your burnt offering, both without defect, and present them before the LORD.'" - Lev 9:2 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Aaron's first act as high priest is to bring a sin offering for himself.

And notice what animal: a bull calf. Aaron had made a golden calf at Sinai, leading the nation into idolatry while Moses was on the mountain (Ex 32:2-4). Now he stands before Israel with a calf in his hands — not as an idol to worship, but as a sacrifice for his sin.

Scripture does not tell us this connection is intentional, so we should not press it too hard. But Aaron would have felt it.

God did not disqualify Aaron for the worst failure of his life. Neither did God let him forget it. He was restored to service, and his service began with honest acknowledgement of his need.

That combination is grace at its most realistic. Not a pretence that the past never happened, and not a permanent exclusion because it did.

Peter, who denied Christ, was restored and told to feed my sheep (Jn 21:17). Paul, who persecuted the church, called himself the worst of sinners while serving as an apostle (1 Tim 1:15).

Your failures are not the end of your usefulness. But you will always serve best as someone who remembers needing mercy.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Has a past failure convinced me I am finished serving God?
2. Do I minister to others out of remembered mercy or out of assumed superiority?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, thank You that You restore people who have failed badly. Let me serve You as someone who has never forgotten Your mercy. Amen.
